Ahijah the Shilonite
ah-HY-jah the SHY-loh-nite
proper noun (a prophet of Shiloh)
Hebrew 'Achiyyah, “brother of the LORD” or “the LORD is my brother,” with ha-Shiloni, the man of Shiloh, the old sanctuary town of Ephraim.

Biblical Definition

Ahijah the Shilonite was a prophet of the LORD from Shiloh, where the tabernacle had stood in the days of Eli, who spoke the word of God at the breaking of the united kingdom and again at the breaking of the house that rent it. Meeting Jeroboam in the way, he clad himself with a new garment and rent it into twelve pieces, bidding the servant of Solomon take ten, for thus saith the LORD: He would rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon—for the idolatry his strange wives had drawn him into—and give ten tribes to Jeroboam, leaving one tribe to David's house for the LORD's servant David's sake and for Jerusalem's sake. Yet the same prophet who promised Jeroboam a sure house if he would walk in God's ways pronounced that house's doom when Jeroboam set up his calves at Bethel and Dan. When Jeroboam's child sickened, he sent his wife in disguise to old and blind Ahijah; but the LORD warned the prophet, and he greeted her at the door with heavy tidings: the child should die, and the dynasty be swept away as a man sweepeth dung. Ahijah is the dictionary's witness that prophecy is no respecter of the powers it once announced: the same mouth that anointed a king for God's purpose condemned him for his apostasy, for the word of the LORD stands above every throne it raises and casts down.

Webster 1828 Definition

The prophet of Shiloh who foretold the division of the kingdom by rending a new garment into twelve pieces for Jeroboam, and afterward pronounced the doom of Jeroboam's house for its idolatry; a witness that the prophetic word judges even the kings it raises.

AHIJAH THE SHILONITE, proper noun. A prophet of the LORD from Shiloh in the reigns of Solomon and Jeroboam.

He met Jeroboam and rent a new garment into twelve pieces, giving him ten as a sign of the ten tribes.

He declared the kingdom rent from Solomon for idolatry, one tribe left to David's house for the LORD's sake.

When Jeroboam fell into the sin of the calves, Ahijah foretold the death of his child and the ruin of his house.

Though blind with age, he knew the disguised queen at the door, for the LORD had shewed him heavy tidings.

Key Scripture

1 Ki 11:31 — "And he said to Jeroboam, Take thee ten pieces: for thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel, Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee."

1 Ki 11:29 — "And it came to pass at that time when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, that the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him in the way; and he had clad himself with a new garment; and they two were alone in the field."

1 Ki 14:6 — "And it was so, when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, that he said, Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam; why feignest thou thyself to be another? for I am sent to thee with heavy tidings."

1 Ki 14:18 — "And they buried him; and all Israel mourned for him, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by the hand of his servant Ahijah the prophet."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the temptation is to admire prophecy only when it flatters a cause and to forget that the same word judges the powers it once anointed.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the impartiality of the prophetic word. Ahijah anointed Jeroboam for a purpose God ordained, the chastening of Solomon's house; the modern habit would then bind the prophet to the man's cause forever. But when Jeroboam corrupted the worship of God with his calves, the same prophet pronounced his ruin. The word of the LORD is no party banner; it raises kings and casts them down by one standard, the obedience of faith.

Ahijah's blindness and his certain knowledge of the disguised queen also rebuke the folly of thinking God can be deceived by appearances. Jeroboam dressed his wife as a stranger, supposing an old and sightless prophet would not know her; but the LORD sees not as man sees, and the prophet greeted her with her own name and heavy tidings at the door. No disguise hides the heart from the God who searches it, and no policy of statecraft outwits the word that has already written the end.

Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew 'Achiyyah, “the LORD is my brother,” with the gentilic ha-Shiloni, marking him a man of Shiloh, the old tabernacle town of Ephraim.

expand to see more

'Ach, Hebrew, brother, joined to Yah, the covenant name, in his proper name.

Shiloh, the Ephraimite town where the tabernacle stood from Joshua until Eli's day.

The rent garment of twelve pieces is an enacted prophecy, common to the prophets, declaring by deed what the word announced.

Davar YHWH, “the word of the LORD,” the phrase that frames both his oracles, the raising and the ruin.

His “heavy tidings” (1 Kings 14:6) name the burden a faithful prophet must carry even to a king's house.

Usage

"He cited Ahijah to show that a true prophet condemns the very king he once anointed when that king forsakes God."

"The teacher noted that the rent garment preached the division of the kingdom before a word of it came to pass."

"“Why feignest thou thyself to be another?” the pastor read, and warned that no disguise hides the heart from God."
